records.destination: 01By hand: both copies of A matterWhich continuous piece of s = ABAAC supplies the two As and one C requested by t = AAC, with the shortest length? A substring is a continuous slice; a window is the slice under consideration. To cover t, each character count must meet its requested count. Their order need not match t.Official bounds: 1 ≤ m,n ≤ 100000, where m and n are the lengths of s and t. Inputs contain English letters; A and a differ. Return an empty string if no window exists. Official tests guarantee a unique answer.Write the positions: 0:A, 1:B, 2:A, 3:A, 4:CInspect windows ending at position 4: [0,4] = ABAAC has A:3, C:1 and length 5. Remove A at position 0: BAAC has A:2, C:1 and length 4. Remove B: AAC has length 3 and still covers. Remove another A: AC has only one A and fails. Fewer than 3 characters cannot supply 3 requested copies, so AAC is shortest. Bounds [left,right] include both endpoints; positions start at 0.A tempting mistake is checking only the set of letters. AC and AAC both contain A and C, yet s = AC, t = AAC has no solution. Stopping at the first covering window also fails: ABAAC covers, but AAC is shorter.Official examples: ADOBECODEBANC / ABC → BANC; a / a → a; a / aa → empty string.A reliable baseline: try every start and endHow can we avoid missing an answer? Fix left, add characters one at a time to the right, check every required count, and kee
